subskill: Integer optimum: coordinate difference of the best plan
prompt:
A workshop builds x chairs and y tables each week, where x and y are whole numbers. Its labor hours and machine hours limit the weekly plan to
5x + 7y ≤ 68
7x + 6y ≤ 84
and its weekly profit, in hundreds of dollars, is P = 5x + 6y. For the plan with the greatest weekly profit, how many more chairs than tables are built?
explanation: The boundary lines 5x + 7y = 68 and 7x + 6y = 84 meet at x = 180/19 ≈ 9.47, y = 56/19 ≈ 2.95, where P ≈ 65.05, so no whole-number plan earns more than 65. Rounding that corner to the nearest whole numbers gives (9, 3), which is allowed (45 + 21 = 66 ≤ 68 and 63 + 18 = 81 ≤ 84) but earns only P = 63; rounding both down gives (9, 2), which earns 57. P = 65 needs 5x + 6y = 65, whose whole-number solutions are (13, 0), (7, 5) and (1, 10): (13, 0) breaks the machine limit (91 > 84), and (7, 5) and (1, 10) break the labor limit (35 + 35 = 70 and 5 + 70 = 75 are more than 68). P = 64 needs 5x + 6y = 64, whose whole-number solutions are (8, 4) and (2, 9); (2, 9) breaks the labor limit (10 + 63 = 73 > 68), and (8, 4) satisfies both (40 + 28 = 68 and 56 + 24 = 80). So the best plan is 8 chairs and 4 tables, and 8 - 4 = 4. Choice 6 rounds the corner to the nearest whole numbers, (9, 3). Choice 7 rounds both corner coordinates down, (9, 2). Choice 12 swaps the two profit rates (P = 6x + 5y), whose best plan is (12, 0).
solve: const ok=(x,y)=>5*x+7*y<=68&&7*x+6*y<=84;let b=-1,bx=0,by=0,n=0;for(let x=0;x<=30;x++)for(let y=0;y<=30;y++)if(ok(x,y)){const v=5*x+6*y;if(v>b){b=v;bx=x;by=y;n=1}else if(v===b)n++}if(n!==1)throw new Error('tie');return bx-by

distractor_solve.12: const ok=(x,y)=>5*x+7*y<=68&&7*x+6*y<=84;let b=-1,bx=0,by=0,n=0;for(let x=0;x<=30;x++)for(let y=0;y<=30;y++)if(ok(x,y)){const v=6*x+5*y;if(v>b){b=v;bx=x;by=y;n=1}else if(v===b)n++}if(n!==1)throw new Error('tie');return bx-by

mechanism: two caps meet at the non-lattice corner (9.47, 2.95)
the rounded plans (9, 3) and (9, 2) are allowed but earn less
test the levels P = 65 (no allowed solution) and P = 64 (only (8, 4))
report x - y of the best plan
quantity_asked: number of chairs minus number of tables in the plan with the greatest profit

setup.i: two capacity limits printed as inequalities in a short workshop model (labor and machine hours)
setup.ii: unique best whole-number plan lies two steps off the rounded corner
setup.iii: difference x - y of the coordinates of the best plan

plugback.why: Ascending, a student tries 4 first. A coordinate difference is shared by many plans ((4, 0), (5, 1), (6, 2), (8, 4), ...), so the option cannot be substituted into the stem; confirming 4 means finding the best plan itself, which is the full solution.

6.why: Rounds the real corner (9.47, 2.95) to the nearest whole numbers, (9, 3), which is allowed, and stops; nothing in the stem shows whether the best plan has a larger or smaller chair surplus.

7.why: Rounds both corner coordinates down, the usual 'stay inside the limits' habit, giving (9, 2); the stem gives no sign which way that moves x - y relative to the best plan.

12.why: Reads the profit as 6 per chair and 5 per table; the swapped objective favours chairs and ends at (12, 0), and a student cannot tell from the stem whether a swapped rate raises or lowers the surplus.

counter_error.solve: const ok=(x,y)=>5*x+7*y<=68&&7*x+6*y<=84;let b=-1,bx=0,by=0,n=0;for(let x=0;x<=30;x++)for(let y=0;y<=30;y++)if(ok(x,y)){const v=5*x+6*y;if(v>b){b=v;bx=x;by=y;n=1}else if(v===b)n++}if(n!==1)throw new Error('tie');return by-bx
counter_error.why: Answering 'how many more tables than chairs' (y - x) gives 4 - 8 = -4, below the key and not an option.

far_distractor.why: Rounding the corner down ordinarily lowers the chair count and so lowers x - y below the corner's 6.5; here y = 2.95 is rounded down by almost a whole table while x loses under half a chair, so (9, 2) lands above the key at 7.

structure_check: The ask is a coordinate difference, not the profit, so 'every slip lowers it' does not apply: answering y - x gives -4 (below), the two rounded plans and the swapped rates land above, and nothing in the item's structure fixes the side. The stem has no universal quantifier; its extremum is on profit, which does not sign errors in x - y.
cheap_bound_check: Cheapest bounds: the machine-hour limit gives x ≤ 12, so x - y ≤ 12; x - y could be negative, so there is no cheap lower bound. All four options (4, 6, 7, 12) survive; the bound strikes no distractor (12 is attained by the allowed plan (12, 0)).
intermediate_check: 6: no - it is the difference for (9, 3); the key needs the level search to (8, 4), not one printed relation. 7: no - the difference for (9, 2); no printed rate maps it to 4. 12: no - the swapped-rate plan (12, 0); nothing printed turns 12 into 4.
shape_check: The stem hands over: x - y is a whole number, at most 12 (machine hours), with no parity or sign condition. All four options are whole numbers from 4 to 12; parity is mixed (4, 6, 12 even; 7 odd). All survive together.
interior_parity_check: Middle values 6 and 7: both one-digit whole numbers, same display form; the key 4 is not interior.
arith_class_check: Key 4 is even like 6 and 12; 7 is odd. 4 is not alone in any class the stem implies (no multiple-of or sign condition).

idea_probe.nearest: e14de4cc-5f0 (live v26 D4, found by the first probe of this slot): a bare system of THREE inequalities including a minimum (y ≥ 3), asking the greatest value of the objective 7x + 6y. Here two capacity limits sit in a workshop model, the optimum is not asked, and the ask is the coordinate difference x - y of the unique best plan (8, 4), off the rounded corners (9, 3) and (9, 2).

self_audit.note: Covering the work, how many options remain legal from the stem alone? All four: x - y ranges over every whole number up to 12, and no option is struck by the machine-hour bound, by parity or by sign. Could a student tell from the stem which way the errors go, and does one bound strike all three? No: y - x gives -4 below while the two roundings and the swapped rates land above; the only cheap bound (x - y ≤ 12) strikes nothing. Could a student confirm an option against the stem in one routine step (key at try 1)? No: many plans share any difference, so 4 can only be confirmed by finding the best plan, which is the whole solution. Is the bypass option really what skipping THIS item's decision point gives? Yes: rounding the real corner (9.47, 2.95) to the nearest whole numbers gives the allowed plan (9, 3) and a difference of 6 (rounding both down gives 7). A test-wise student who computes the real corner (difference about 6.5) sees 6 and 7 beside it; that needs the corner computation and points away from the key. No option is the sum, difference or mean of two others (4 + 6 = 10, 12 - 7 = 5, 12 - 6 = 6 uses 6 twice; none is a third option). Preflight (read) lines: PAIR 4 + 6 = 10 = 2 x 5, DPAIR/DSUM 4 + 7 = 11 = 5 + 6 and 12 - 4 = 8 = 7 + 1 are coincidences of the small printed coefficients; no stem reading moves between plan differences by those numbers. D4 (the word greatest) is on the profit, not on the asked difference, whose errors go both ways (-4 below; 6, 7, 12 above).
